--- content ---
---
kicker: MAIIC IFRS 9 and EIR system
title: Connecting the IFRS 9 system to E-Banker
subtitle: A plain-language guide to the data-access request
date: 14 October 2026
prepared: Edward Mazibuko, Director, Data Analytics, Dupleix Institute
people: For Dr Thomson Kumwenda (CFO), MAIIC management and Finance; the technical version is the data-access request of the same date
status: Draft for discussion
---

## 1. The short version

MAIIC's new IFRS 9 system calculates expected credit losses, interest revenue and the regulatory figures from the loan data held in E-Banker, MAIIC's banking system. Today that data is copied out of E-Banker **by hand**: Barry runs a set of queries every month, saves the results as files and shares them with us. It works, but it is slow, depends on one person, and has gone wrong several times in small ways that each cost a re-run.

We are asking MAIIC to let the IFRS 9 system **read** the data from E-Banker automatically, using a special login that can **look but never change anything**. We would set it up and test it on a copy of E-Banker first, and only switch it on for the real system once it has proved itself. The hand method stays available as a backup.

What we need: Dr Thom's approval, a login created by Barry's team, and written confirmation from Virtual Galaxy (the company that supplies E-Banker) that this does not affect their support.

## 2. Why change

Every monthly batch of data so far has needed a second attempt for one of three reasons:

- the date format was not set before the queries ran, so dates arrived in the wrong format;
- the export tool stopped part-way because a file was too big, and produced a file that looked complete but was not;
- one table (E-Banker's daily overdue calculation) is simply too large to copy out by hand.

An automatic read avoids all three. It also means the data arrives on time each month without anyone having to remember to run it.

## 3. The five ways data can reach the system

There are five ways the data can travel from E-Banker to the IFRS 9 system. They differ only in **who** fetches the data and **how** it travels. Whatever the way, the data ends up in the same place and is checked in the same way.

| Way | In everyday terms | Where it stands |
|---|---|---|
| **1. By hand** | Barry runs the queries and shares the files | What happens today |
| **2. Scheduled script** | A small program on a MAIIC computer fetches the data at a set time each month and drops the files in a shared folder | Ready on our side; needs the login and the folder |
| **3. Sent over the internet** | The same program sends the files straight to the system instead of using a folder | Ready on our side; needs a security key |
| **4. The system reads it directly** (what we are asking for) | The IFRS 9 system connects to E-Banker itself, over the secure link that already exists, and fetches the data | About a week to build once the login exists |
| **5. Through the vendor** | Virtual Galaxy provides a ready-made window onto the data, and the system reads that | Only if the vendor will not allow way 4; likely a paid job |

Ways 2 and 4 use the **same login**, so we would start with way 2 (no new software anywhere) while waiting for the vendor's agreement to way 4.

![Figure 1. Five ways in, one checkpoint. Whatever way the data travels, it passes the same checks before the system uses it.](Feed routes and landing zone - diagram.png)

## 4. The "landing zone": a checkpoint at the door

All data from E-Banker passes through one checkpoint inside the system before anything is calculated from it. We call it the **landing zone**. Think of it as a receiving bay in a warehouse: every delivery is counted and inspected before it goes onto the shelves, and a delivery that fails inspection is set aside, not used.

At the checkpoint the system:

- **counts and fingerprints every file**, to be sure it is complete and is the file E-Banker produced;
- **checks that the pieces fit together**, for example that every loan payment belongs to a loan the system knows about, and that the loan balances agree with the general ledger;
- **refuses a delivery that fails**, keeping it aside so the problem can be seen, but never letting it reach the figures;
- **keeps every version of every record**, so if E-Banker later changes a record, the old version is still there. Any month reported in the past can be reproduced exactly as it was.

This is what makes the change safe: switching from the hand method to the automatic read changes nothing about how the figures are calculated, only how the data arrives.

## 5. The login we are asking for

Barry's team would create one login on E-Banker's database with these limits:

- it can **read** a fixed list of tables (the loan accounts, their payments, balances and repayment schedules, and the trial balance) and **nothing else**;
- it **cannot change, add or delete** anything, and cannot run any of E-Banker's programs;
- it only reads the records of MAIIC's own loan schemes and the Mega Farm programme;
- it can only connect from one named computer, over the secure link MAIIC already has;
- MAIIC holds the password, changes it every 90 days, can see everything the login does, and can switch it off at any moment.

The technical document gives Barry's team the exact steps and a short test to prove the login really is read-only before it is handed over.

## 6. What we need from the vendor

The login is within MAIIC's own control, but we ask Virtual Galaxy to confirm in writing that it does not affect their support agreement; whether they prefer us to read a copy of the database rather than the live one; whether they need any extra logging; and whether there is any cost. If they will not allow it, we ask them to quote for way 5 instead.

## 7. Test first, then go live

Nothing touches the real E-Banker data until the whole arrangement has worked on a copy.

1. **Approve.** Dr Thom approves; Barry asks the vendor.
2. **Test on a copy.** Barry's team creates the login on E-Banker's test copy. We connect it to the IFRS 9 system's own test copy (the "bootstrap", below). We run way 2, then way 4, and check seven things together, including that nothing outside the agreed list can be read, that the automatic read gives exactly the same data as the hand method, and that a broken file is caught.
3. **Go live.** The login is created on the real E-Banker, and the setting in the system is switched to way 4, which needs two people to approve.
4. **Run side by side.** For two month-ends, both the hand method and the automatic read are used, and they must agree exactly before the hand method is retired. It remains available as a backup.

## 8. The bootstrap: our test copy and safety check

The **bootstrap** is a single command in the IFRS 9 system that builds a complete copy of the system from scratch, on a separate test database, in about two minutes. It loads every batch of data MAIIC has sent, runs every calculation, and then checks nine key figures that must agree exactly with an independent source (for example, that the loan balances agree with the trial balance on each loan account in the general ledger). Today all nine agree. It never touches the real system, and nothing approved inside it counts as a MAIIC approval.

It plays four parts in this project: it is the **test copy** the automatic read is first connected to; it is the **yardstick**, because the automatic read must reproduce exactly what arrived by hand; it is the **safety check** run before any change reaches the live system; and it is the **fire drill** for restoring the system from backup each quarter.

![Figure 2. The bootstrap builds the system on a test copy and checks nine key figures; only when they agree does a change reach the live system.](Bootstrap - test harness and reference copy - diagram.png)

## 9. Keeping the data safe

- **Storage.** The data is small: the whole system takes about 110 MB today and should stay under 2 GB for five years. It is kept permanently, because past figures must be reproducible; that is longer than the seven years required for accounting records.
- **Backups.** A full copy every night, kept off the server; a permanent copy each time a month is closed; a test restore every quarter. Backups are encrypted, and MAIIC holds the keys.
- **Duplicates.** If the same data arrives twice, it is recognised and not counted twice.
- **Control.** Which way the data arrives is a setting that needs two people to change. Changes to the queries go through a controlled process, and an out-of-date query is refused. Every delivery, accepted or refused, is recorded.

## 10. What we are asking MAIIC to do

| Who | What |
|---|---|
| Dr Thom | Approve the request |
| Barry and ICT | Create the read-only login, first on the test copy and later on the live system, following the steps in the technical document; open the network path from one computer |
| Barry | Ask Virtual Galaxy for written confirmation (section 6) |
| Dupleix | Build the automatic read, run the tests with Barry, and run the two month-ends side by side |

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **E-Banker** | MAIIC's core banking system, where loans, payments and the general ledger are recorded. Supplied and supported by Virtual Galaxy. |
| **IFRS 9 system** | The system Dupleix is building for MAIIC to calculate expected credit losses, interest revenue and the regulatory figures from E-Banker's data. |
| **Oracle** | The database software E-Banker stores its data in. |
| **Database** | The organised store of records behind a system. E-Banker has one; the IFRS 9 system has its own. |
| **Production (live)** | The real system and data used for MAIIC's reporting. |
| **Test environment (test copy, UAT)** | A separate copy of a system used for trying things out, so mistakes cannot affect the real data. |
| **Replica (standby)** | A continuously updated copy of the live database, often used for reporting so the live system is not disturbed. |
| **Query** | A precise request for data from a database, such as "all payments on MAIIC's loans since 1 September". |
| **Read-only login (account)** | A username and password that can look at data but cannot change it. |
| **Grant** | Permission given to a login to read a particular table. |
| **Table** | One set of records in a database, such as the list of loan accounts or the list of payments. |
| **VPN** | A secure, encrypted connection between two organisations' networks. MAIIC already has one with Dupleix. |
| **Firewall** | The network gatekeeper that decides which computers may connect to which. |
| **Feed route** | The way data travels from E-Banker to the IFRS 9 system (one of the five in section 3). |
| **Pack** | One delivery of data: one file per query, plus a list of what the files should contain. |
| **Manifest** | The list that comes with each pack, stating how many records each file holds and its fingerprint. |
| **Hash (fingerprint)** | A short code calculated from a file's exact contents. If even one character changes, the code changes, so it proves a file is complete and unaltered. |
| **Landing zone** | The checkpoint inside the IFRS 9 system where every delivery is checked and stored before any calculation uses it. |
| **Gates (checks)** | The tests every delivery must pass at the landing zone. |
| **Quarantine** | Setting aside a delivery that failed a check: kept for inspection, never used. |
| **Version** | A record as it stood at a point in time. When E-Banker changes a record, the system keeps the old version and adds the new one. |
| **Watermark** | A marker of the last record already received, so the next delivery only fetches what is new. |
| **Bootstrap** | The command that rebuilds the whole IFRS 9 system from scratch on a test database and checks the key figures. |
| **Golden ties** | The nine key figures the bootstrap checks against an independent source; all must agree exactly. |
| **Maker-checker** | A control where one person proposes a change and a second person must approve it. |
| **Period lock** | Closing a reporting month so its figures cannot change afterwards. |
| **Audit trail** | The record of who or what did what, and when, kept for the auditors. |
| **Trial balance** | The list of every general ledger account's balance at a date, produced by Finance from E-Banker. |
| **Mega Farm** | The farming programme whose loans MAIIC administers alongside its own loan book. |
| **Virtual Galaxy** | The company that supplies and supports E-Banker. |
| **Dupleix** | Dupleix Institute, the firm building the IFRS 9 system for MAIIC. |

````

38	        $folder = (string) ($this->argument('folder') ?? config('services.ebanker_feed.folder'));

41	            return self::SUCCESS;

49	        $candidates = [];
50	        if (is_file($folder . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . 'manifest.json')) {
51	            $candidates[] = $folder;
52	        }
53	        foreach (glob($folder . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . '*', GLOB_ONLYDIR) ?: [] as $sub) {
54	            if (is_file($sub . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . 'manifest.json')) {
55	                $candidates[] = $sub;
56	            }
57	        }
58	        if ($this->option('also-route-3')) {

The alternative to route 2 where a shared folder between the two servers is awkward |")

route3 = """### 3.1 Route 3 in detail: the endpoint

An **endpoint** is an address on the IFRS 9 system's web server that accepts a delivery from another computer, in the way a web page accepts a form. Route 3 uses one: `POST https://<system server>/api/ebanker-feed/pack`. The MAIIC script runs the same queries as under route 2; the only difference is that instead of leaving the pack in a shared folder, it sends it straight to this address. Figure 3 shows the exchange.

![Figure 3. Route 3: the MAIIC script reads E-Banker, then posts the zipped pack to the system's endpoint; the endpoint checks it on arrival and replies at once; the landing zone lands it at the next poll through the same gates as every route.](Route 3 - push by API endpoint - sequence diagram.png)

**What the endpoint does with each delivery, in order** (this is how it is built today):

| Step | What happens | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| 1. The token | The request must carry `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The token is compared with the one configured on the system's server (`EBANKER_FEED_TOKEN`), in a way that does not leak its length or content through timing | Refused with 401; nothing is stored |
| 2. The file | The body must carry one file, field name `pack`, which must be a readable zip | Refused with 422 |
| 3. The names inside the zip | Every entry name is checked before anything is written; a name that would write outside the inbox (for example `../../`) refuses the whole zip, and the attempt is logged with the sender's IP | Refused with 422; logged as a warning |
| 4. The manifest | The zip must hold `manifest.json` (at the top or in one sub-folder) | Refused with 422 |
| 5. Into the inbox | The zip is unpacked into its own inbox folder named by date, time and the first characters of the file's hash; an audit entry "E-Banker Pack Received by API" records the inbox and the sender's IP | |
| 6. The reply | `202 Accepted`, with the inbox name. 202 means **received, not yet landed** | |
| 7. The landing | At the next run of the poller (daily at 06:30, `eir:poll-feed-folder --also-route-3`), the pack goes through the landing zone exactly as under every other route: the gates, landed or quarantined, versioned rows, watermarks. The load is recorded as route `ROUTE_3_API` | Quarantined, with the failures named |

A pack sent twice is recognised by its manifest hash at step 7 and not landed twice (section 11).

**Push and pull: who opens the connection.** This is usually what decides between the routes, because it decides which firewall rule MAIIC's ICT has to open.

| Route | Who starts it | Connection opened | Firewall rule needed | Where the E-Banker password lives | What the system holds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Manual | A person | Barry to E-Banker; then a browser upload to the system | None new | With Barry | Nothing |
| 2. Scheduled export | MAIIC's scheduled task | MAIIC server to E-Banker; MAIIC server to a shared folder the system can read | A share both servers can reach | Oracle Wallet on the MAIIC server | Read access to the folder |
| 3. Push by API (endpoint) | MAIIC's scheduled task | MAIIC server to E-Banker; MAIIC server **out** to the system over HTTPS | Outbound HTTPS (443) from the MAIIC server to the system's server | Oracle Wallet on the MAIIC server | The feed token only |
| 4. Direct read | The system's scheduler | System server **in** to E-Banker over the VPN | Inbound to the database listener (1521) from the system's server | The system server's configuration | The read-only database password |
| 5. Vendor view or API | The system's scheduler | System server to the vendor's views or the vendor's own endpoint | As route 4, or to the vendor's endpoint | The system server's configuration | The vendor's credentials |

Routes 2 and 3 keep every connection to E-Banker inside MAIIC: the IFRS 9 system never connects into MAIIC's network and never holds an E-Banker password. That makes them the natural choice if MAIIC's ICT policy does not allow an outside system to connect to the database. Route 4 is simpler to run (nothing to install at MAIIC) but needs the inbound rule.

**Route 5's endpoint is a different thing.** Under route 5 the endpoint would be the vendor's, not ours: Virtual Galaxy would publish an address the system calls to fetch the data (a pull), and the system would need a small connector written to their specification. That is only worth doing if the vendor refuses route 4 and MAIIC prefers not to run a script (routes 2 and 3).

**What would be added before route 3 goes live.** The endpoint works today, but four hardening items would be added if route 3 is chosen, about a day's work:

- **An IP allow-list**, so only the MAIIC server's address is accepted (today any address with the token is). Until then, the same can be done on the system server's firewall.
- **Two-token rotation**, so a new token can be issued and the old one retired without a gap (today there is one token in the configuration).
- **Landing on receipt**, so the reply can say "landed" or "quarantined" straight away instead of waiting for the 06:30 poll; or the poll run more often on the first working days of the month.
- **A size limit and a status address**, so oversize packs are refused clearly (today the limit is the web server's upload limit, which must be raised to at least 100 MB) and the script can ask for the result of its last delivery.

"""

# setup: route 3 steps after route 2's step 9

The script sends each pack with the built-in Windows command `curl.exe -f -X POST "https://<system server>/api/ebanker-feed/pack" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -F "pack=@<pack>.zip"`, writes the reply to its log, and tries again up to three times if the reply is not 202. **Step 10. Look after the account.**""")

plain3 = """### Way 3 explained: the "letterbox"

The IFRS 9 system has a secure address on its web server that accepts deliveries of data, rather like a locked letterbox. In technical terms it is called an **endpoint**. Under way 3, MAIIC's small program fetches the data from E-Banker, packs it into a single compressed file, and posts it to this letterbox over an encrypted connection, together with a long secret code (the **token**) that proves it comes from MAIIC.

The letterbox checks four things the moment a delivery arrives: that the secret code is right, that the file is a proper compressed file, that nothing inside it is trying to write where it should not, and that it carries its list of contents. If any check fails, the delivery is refused on the spot. If all pass, the system replies "received" straight away and puts the delivery in a holding tray. Early the next morning the system takes it through the same checkpoint as every other delivery (section 4) before any figure uses it.

The main attraction of way 3 is that **MAIIC makes every connection itself**. The IFRS 9 system never connects into MAIIC's network and never holds an E-Banker password; it only holds the secret code for its own letterbox. If MAIIC's policy is that no outside system may connect to the banking database, ways 2 and 3 meet it; way 4 does not.

![Figure 3. Way 3 step by step: the MAIIC program reads E-Banker, posts the packed file to the system's letterbox, the letterbox checks it and replies at once, and the checkpoint takes it in the next morning.](Route 3 - push by API endpoint - sequence diagram.png)

Before way 3 is used for real, we would add four safeguards, about a day's work: accept deliveries only from MAIIC's server, allow the secret code to be changed without a gap, take deliveries through the checkpoint as soon as they arrive, and refuse oversized deliveries clearly.

"""
p = sub(p, "## 4. The \"landing zone\": a checkpoint at the door", plain3 + "## 4. The \"landing zone\": a checkpoint at the door")
gl = """| **API** | A way for one computer system to send requests or data to another automatically, without a person in between. |
| **Endpoint ("letterbox")** | A specific secure address on a system that accepts deliveries or requests from another computer. The IFRS 9 system's endpoint for E-Banker data is `/api/ebanker-feed/pack`. |
| **Token** | A long secret code sent with each delivery to prove who it comes from, like a password for a computer rather than a person. |
| **HTTPS** | The encrypted form of web traffic (the padlock in a browser), so data cannot be read on the way. |
| **Push and pull** | Push: the sender delivers the data (ways 2 and 3, MAIIC sends). Pull: the receiver fetches it (ways 4 and 5, the IFRS 9 system fetches). It decides which side opens the connection. |
| **202 Accepted** | The reply the letterbox gives when a delivery is received and waiting to be checked; not yet a confirmation that it passed the checks. |
"""
p = sub(p, "| **Feed route** |", gl + "| **Feed route** |")

## CLAUDE  (2026-10-14 12:59:01 UTC)

Yes. The landing zone has a fixed schema of four tables, created by `database/migrations/2026_10_08_000000_create_ebanker_landing_zone.php` and adjusted by two later migrations. The design is a hybrid, though: the **envelope** around each record has a fixed, typed schema, while **E-Banker's own columns** are stored verbatim as JSON inside it.

**The four tables**

| Table | One row per | Typed columns | Keys and indexes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ebanker_queries` (the register) | Registered query (P1_01, P2_08, OD_01 …) | `query_id`, `title`, `source_table`, `key_column`, `account_column`, `date_column`, `version`, `sql`, `sha256`, `incremental` | `query_id` unique |
| `ebanker_loads` | Pack | `pack_hash` (SHA-256 of the manifest), `pack_name`, `route` (ROUTE_1_MANUAL … ROUTE_5_VENDOR), `period`, `run_at`, `date_format`, `manifest` (JSON), `gates` (JSON), `status` (PENDING / LANDED / QUARANTINED), `watermarks` (JSON), `loaded_by`, `loaded_at` | `pack_hash` unique (so the same pack can't land twice) |
| `ebanker_pack_files` | File in a pack | `load_id`, `file`, `query_id`, `query_version`, `sha256`, `rows_declared`, `rows_loaded`, `rows_new`, `rows_versioned`, `rows_unchanged`, `status`, `note` | `(load_id, file)` unique; foreign key to loads |
| `ebanker_raw_rows` | Version of a source record | `load_id`, `query_id`, `source_key` (E-Banker's own id, e.g. CUMVOUCH_DET_ID), `account`, `row_date` (parsed once at landing), **`payload` (JSON: every column of the E-Banker row, verbatim)**, `row_hash`, `version`, `superseded_at` | `(load_id, query_id, source_key)` unique; indexes on `(query_id, source_key)`, `(query_id, row_date)` and `account`; covering index `(query_id, superseded_at, load_id, row_date)`, added 13 Oct for speed |

**Why the E-Banker columns are JSON rather than one typed table per E-Banker table**

- **One loader for every query.** About 60 queries over 37 E-Banker tables all go through the same code. Adding a new query (OD_02 today) needs a line in the register, not a database migration.
- **A vendor change doesn't break the landing.** If Virtual Galaxy adds a column, the row still lands with it. If they rename or drop one, the gates and the dictionary extract (DD_03) catch it before a build reads it.
- **Evidence.** The row is kept exactly as E-Banker produced it, with a hash. Nothing is lost by converting it into our types at the door.
- The fields every reader needs (key, account, date, version, current or superseded) are pulled out into **typed, indexed columns**, so the system never has to search inside the JSON to find a row.

**Where the typed schema takes over.** The builds read the payloads once per run and convert them into the system's strongly typed working tables: `loan_books`, contract inputs, fees, `gl_trial_balance_lines`, EIR schedules and so on. Each of those has a full column-by-column schema. So the system is schema-on-read inside the landing zone (the structure is applied when the data is read) and schema-on-write from the builds onwards (the structure is enforced when the data is stored).

The trade-off is that querying the raw JSON directly is slower than querying a typed table. That's why the builds read each query's rows once and slice them in memory, and why the covering index was added.

The data-access request's §4 only names these four tables. I can add a short annex with this table if Barry's team or the auditors would want to see the structure.

Yes. All four landing-zone tables exist in both test databases, and they hold data:

| Table | Bootstrap (`maiic_ifrs9_bootstrap`) | Demo (`maiic_ifrs9_demo`) |
|---|---:|---:|
| `ebanker_queries` (register) | 65 queries | 64 queries |
| `ebanker_loads` (packs) | 23 | 2 |
| `ebanker_pack_files` | 75 | 54 |
| `ebanker_raw_rows` | 88,977 | 85,174 |

- **Bootstrap.** It was one migration behind: the 13 October speed index on the raw rows had not been applied, along with the go-live migrations a colleague pushed today (go-live controls, restructure register, reopen/unlock requests). I've just applied them, so the bootstrap is now fully up to date with 0 pending.

import re, shutil, subprocess, sys
from pathlib import Path
DIR = Path(r"C:\Users\wadza\OneDrive\2026\Projects\MAIIC\3. Project Execution\E-Banker Integration")
REPO = Path(r"C:\xampp\htdocs\MAICC-IFRS9")
TECH = DIR / "Data access request - E-Banker read-only access (route 4) - 14 Oct 2026.md"
PLAIN = DIR / "Plain-language guide - connecting the IFRS 9 system to E-Banker - 14 Oct 2026.md"
FIG4 = "Landing zone - the four tables, one payment followed through - diagram.png"

def sub(t, a, b):
    assert a in t, "anchor missing: " + a[:80]
    return t.replace(a, b, 1)

t = TECH.read_text(encoding="utf-8")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 4.1 the four tables, as a lesson
lesson = f"""### 4.1 Inside the landing zone: the four tables, explained

This part is written so that anyone at MAIIC can follow it, not only ICT. If you have run a receiving office, you already know how the landing zone is organised: it keeps four record books.

1. **The register** (`ebanker_queries`) is the list of everything the system is allowed to ask E-Banker for: about sixty questions, each with a code (P1_01, P2_08, OD_01 …). For each one it records which E-Banker table it reads, which column is that table's own unique number for a record, which columns hold the account and the date, the version of the question, and whether to fetch everything each time or only what is new. If a question is not in the register, the system will not accept its answers.
2. **The deliveries book** (`ebanker_loads`) has one line for every pack that arrives: when, by which route, its fingerprint, whether it was accepted (LANDED) or set aside (QUARANTINED), the result of every check, and the **watermark**, meaning the last record received for each question so that the next delivery fetches only what is new.
3. **The files book** (`ebanker_pack_files`) has one line for every file inside a pack: its fingerprint, how many records the pack said it held, how many were actually stored, and how many of those were new, changed or already held.
4. **The records book** (`ebanker_raw_rows`) holds the records themselves, one line for each version of each E-Banker record. A few facts are copied into labelled columns so they can be found quickly: E-Banker's own record number, the account, the date, the version, and whether this version has been replaced. The full record, every column exactly as E-Banker sent it, is kept beside them unchanged.

**One real payment, followed through** (Figure 4, from the bootstrap database). MUSECO repaid K200,000,000 on 24 July 2025. In E-Banker that is ledger record 194427. It arrived in delivery 1 (by hand, accepted on 9 October 2026), in the file `P1_01_ledger_all.csv`. That file said it held 3,640 records and 3,640 were stored. In the records book it is line 20: account 000104420000005, dated 24 July 2025, version 1, not replaced, with all 83 of E-Banker's columns kept as they were (amount 200,000,000.00, transaction type 305, "By Trf Loan repayment", loan GL 1050101).

![Figure 4. The four record books of the landing zone, following MUSECO's K200,000,000 repayment of 24 July 2025 from E-Banker's ledger to line 20 of the records book, and what happens if E-Banker later corrects it.](Landing zone - the four tables, one payment followed through - diagram.png)

**What happens if E-Banker later changes that record.** Suppose the payment is corrected in E-Banker to K195,000,000. At the next delivery the system sees record 194427 again with a different fingerprint. It does **not** overwrite line 20. It marks line 20 with the date and time it was replaced, and adds a new line, version 2, holding the corrected amount. Figures already reported for October were calculated from version 1 and can be reproduced exactly; figures from November use version 2. If the record arrives again unchanged, its fingerprint matches and nothing is added. (So far no record has needed a second version; the figure shows the case as an illustration.)

**Questions MAIIC can answer from the four books**, without asking Dupleix:

| Question | Where the answer is |
|---|---|
| Did this month's pack arrive, and was it accepted? | The deliveries book: the pack's line, its status and its check results |
| Was any file short or altered? | The files book: records declared against records stored, and the fingerprint |
| Which E-Banker record is behind a figure in a report? | The records book: E-Banker's record number, the delivery it came in, its version |
| Has E-Banker changed a record we had already received? | The records book: any line with a version above 1, and the date its earlier version was replaced |
| What exactly did we ask E-Banker for, and has the question changed? | The register: the query, its version and the fingerprint of its SQL |

**Have the tables been created?** Yes, in the system's test databases, where they hold the data received so far: the bootstrap database holds 65 registered questions, 23 deliveries, 75 files and 88,977 records. This route has to be planned early. The build itself is about a week; the time is taken by things outside the build, most of them outside Dupleix's control, and each one can only happen in a fixed order:

- **Approvals and the vendor take weeks, not days.** Dr Thom's authorisation, the vendor's written confirmation of support terms, and MAIIC's own change control for a new database account and a firewall rule all have to be in place before anything can be tested.
- **A test copy of E-Banker has to exist.** If MAIIC does not already have a UAT copy, one has to be restored from a backup; that is ICT and vendor time that needs booking.
- **Proof needs real month-ends, and there is only one a month.** The parallel run needs two month-ends read both ways and tying row for row. If the November month-end is missed, the earliest switch moves from January to February; every missed month-end moves it by a full month.
- **Year-end is the month that matters most.** The December 2026 year-end feeds the annual financial statements and Deloitte's audit. Having route 4 proven on November and run in parallel on December gives the auditors the strongest evidence: the same figures by two independent routes. Starting later means the year-end is read by hand only.
- **Year-end change freezes.** Many ICT teams freeze changes over December. Everything that changes MAIIC's systems (the accounts, the firewall rule, the production set-up) is therefore scheduled to finish by **27 November**.
- **The manual route carries risk every month it remains the only one.** Each pack so far has needed a re-run; the overdue table cannot be exported by hand at all. Until route 2 or 4 is live, those risks recur at every month-end.

**What was added**

1. **The landing-zone tables, explained step by step.** This is technical §4.1, with a short version in the guide.
   - The four tables are described as four record books: the register, the deliveries book, the files book and the records book.
   - **Figure 4** follows one real payment through all four: MUSECO's K200,000,000 repayment of 24 July 2025, which is E-Banker record 194427, arriving as line 20 of delivery 1 (3,640 of 3,640 rows stored).
   - A worked "what if E-Banker corrects it" example shows that version 1 is kept and marked as replaced, and version 2 is added beside it.
   - A table of questions MAIIC can answer from the four books without asking Dupleix.
   - Whether the tables exist yet: yes in the test databases (65 queries, 23 deliveries, 75 files, 88,977 records); in production they are created empty at installation.
2. **Connection test, as setup step 6a.**
   - A network check: `Test-NetConnection … -Port 1521`.
   - A login check from SQLcl or SQL Developer.
   - The **test-connection query**: who you're connected as, which database, which service, from which IP, and the database time. It must name the *test* database at stage B and production at stage C.
   - A first data read: a count of MAIIC loan accounts.
   - The results are saved as evidence, re-run at production (step 11), and included in acceptance test 1.
3. **Plan early, and the timetable.**
   - A "Please plan this now" paragraph at the top of both documents.
   - §9.1 sets out six reasons it has to start now: approvals and the vendor take weeks; a test copy of E-Banker must exist; proof needs real month-ends; the December year-end feeds the audit; ICT year-end change freezes; and the manual route stays a risk every month until it's replaced.

|---|---|

| Switch | 18–22 Jan |
| First month-end by route 4 alone | Mon 1 Feb 2027 |

   If the vendor doesn't reply by 6 November, the same dates continue on route 2.

369:Changing a query (a column added, a filter corrected) means a **new version in the register**. Each pack's manifest states the version of every file in it; a file whose version is not the one the register holds is refused (the `query_version` gate), so an old script cannot feed the system unnoticed. 279	## 8. The bootstrap: how the integration is tested before production
280	
281	**What the bootstrap is.** One command in the IFRS 9 system, `eir:bootstrap`, that rebuilds the whole system from scratch on a separate, throwaway database (`maiic_ifrs9_bootstrap`) and proves the result. It takes about two minutes and never touches the production database (`maiic_ifrs9`). It has been run after every change since 8 October; it is how the figures in every review and audit to date were produced.
282	
283	**What it does, in order.**
284	
285	1. **Wipe.** Empties the test database and creates it again from the system's own definitions.
286	2. **Land.** Takes every pack MAIIC has sent so far (kept, with their hashes, in the project repository) and the client inputs (Finance's fee template, the take-on workbook, the trial balances), and lands them through the same landing zone and the same gates as production (section 4).
287	3. **Build.** Builds the monthly loan books, the contract inputs, the fees and the EIR schedules from the landed rows.
288	4. **Run the engines.** Staging, PD and LGD, ECL, EIR and revenue, the forward-looking chain, sensitivity and stress, the reports, the compliance register and the GL reconciliation, month by month, in the same order as production.
289	5. **Verify.** Checks nine **golden ties**: figures that must agree exactly with an independent source. They are the interest posted in the ledger; the carrying amount against E-Banker's stored loan book report, for every account and month; the year-end interest contra entries on GL 4215 and 4216; and the loan book against the trial balance on the five loan GLs (1050101, 1050102, 1050201, 1050202, 1050401). 401	| The pack files themselves (CSV and manifest, under the manual and folder routes) | The files as E-Banker produced them, kept for evidence | 87 MB received to date on OneDrive |
402	
403	**Growth.** On the MAIIC book a month adds roughly 3 to 5 MB to the landing zone. Two items change the scale and are planned for:
404	
405	- **The Mega Farm ledger** (about 300,000 postings, not yet landed in full) adds an estimated 300 to 400 MB once, then a few MB a month.
406	- **The daily overdue run** (OD_02) adds about 45,000 rows a year for the MAIIC schemes (an estimated 120 to 150 MB a year). The Mega Farm programme has 3,675 accounts, so its daily rows would be about 1.3 million a year; for Mega Farm the system reads the **month-end rows only**, and the daily read stays limited to the MAIIC schemes.
407	
408	On that basis the database stays **under 2 GB for the first five years**. The server needs **at least 20 GB of free disk** for the database, its backups held locally and the pack archive, with an alert at 80 percent full.
409	
410	**Retention.** Landed rows and pack records are kept for the life of the system and never deleted: the superseded versions are what let a reported month be re-derived exactly as it was, which the auditors rely on. This exceeds the seven-year minimum for accounting records. Pack files may be archived off the server after the month they belong to is locked, because the landing zone holds every row and every file's hash.
411	
412	**Backup.**
413	
414	| What | How often | Kept | Where |
415	|---|---|---|---|
416	| Full database dump (compressed; about 10 MB today) | Nightly, after the 06:30 feed run has finished | 30 daily, 12 month-end, 7 year-end copies | On the server, and copied off it to MAIIC's backup store (a second site or MAIIC's cloud) |
417	| Month-end snapshot, taken when the month is locked | Monthly | Permanently | Off the server, alongside the month's pack files |
418	| The pack files and manifests | As each pack lands | Permanently | MAIIC's document store (OneDrive today) |
419	| The query register and the system code | On every change | The full history | The private repository, which MAIIC holds a copy of |
420	
421	Every backup is **encrypted at rest**: the data is customer loan data. A **restore test** is run each quarter: the latest dump restored to a separate database, the bootstrap's tie checks run against it, and the result recorded. The database password, the read-only E-Banker password and the backup encryption key are held by MAIIC ICT, not by Dupleix.
422	
423	**If the system's database is lost**, it is restored from the last nightly dump; anything landed after it is re-read from E-Banker, because the watermarks in the restored database say where to start, and the duplicate rules (section 11) make a re-read safe.
424	
425	## 14. Contact
426	
427	Edward Mazibuko, Director, Data Analytics, Dupleix Institute. Technical questions from the vendor can come to us directly, copied to Barry.

body = body[:gs] + "- `CREATE ROLE ifrs9_feed_read;`\n" + grants + "\n" + body[ge:]
print(len(tables), "grant lines;", len(set(tables)), "distinct")

t = head + body
assert "Barry" not in body

file_path: C:\Users\wadza\OneDrive\2026\Projects\MAIIC\3. Project Execution\E-Banker Integration\Plain-language guide - connecting the IFRS 9 system to E-Banker - 14 Oct 2026.md
--- content ---
---
kicker: MAIIC IFRS 9 and EIR system
title: Connecting the IFRS 9 system to E-Banker
date: 14 October 2026
prepared: Edward Mazibuko, Director, Data Analytics, Dupleix Institute
people: For Dr Thomson Kumwenda (CFO), MAIIC management, Finance and ICT; the technical version is the data-access request of the same date, and the two follow the same sections
status: Draft for discussion
logo: Dupleix logo.png
justify: yes
---

## 1. What we are asking for

MAIIC's IFRS 9 system calculates expected credit losses, interest revenue and the regulatory figures from the loan data held in E-Banker, MAIIC's banking system. Today that data is copied out of E-Banker by hand each month. We are asking MAIIC to let the IFRS 9 system **read** the data from E-Banker automatically, using a special login that can **look but never change anything**.

In practice this means five things from MAIIC:

1. A **read-only login** on E-Banker's database that can read a fixed list of tables and nothing else.
2. Permission in MAIIC's **firewall** for one computer, the IFRS 9 system's server on MAIIC's own network, to reach the database.
3. The **connection details** (the database's address and name), and a short session to test them with MAIIC ICT present.
4. If E-Banker keeps a **copy of the live database** for reporting, the login on that copy rather than the live one, so the live system is never disturbed.
5. The same login **first on E-Banker's test copy**, so everything is proved there before it touches real data.

**Please plan this now.** The building work is about a week, but approvals, the vendor's reply, a test copy of E-Banker and two months of running the old and new methods side by side take the time. To have the new method proven before the December 2026 year-end, which feeds the annual accounts and the audit, we need approval by **Friday 23 October 2026** (timetable in section 9.2).

## 2. Why change

Every monthly batch of data so far has needed a second attempt for one of three reasons: the date format was not set before the queries ran; the export tool stopped part-way because a file was too big, producing a file that looked complete but was not; or a table (E-Banker's daily overdue calculation) was simply too large to copy out by hand. An automatic read avoids all three, arrives on time each month, and does not depend on one person remembering to run it.

The system already keeps a record of every delivery: what was asked for, how many records came, a fingerprint of each file and the checks it passed. An automatic read keeps exactly the same record, so the auditors see the same trail whichever way a month arrived.

### 2.1 Where things stand (14 October 2026)

- **How the data is copied today.** MAIIC ICT runs the queries on its own computer while Dupleix watches the screen over AnyDesk. MAIIC keeps its hands on its own database, and Dupleix can correct a setting on the spot. Ten batches have been run this way; the tenth was prepared on 14 October as the system was being built.
- **The system is moving onto MAIIC's server.** MAIIC ICT now has access to the system's code and has already copied it onto a MAIIC server. The first thing run there is the **bootstrap** (section 8), which rebuilds the system from every batch received so far and checks nine key figures, proving the installation before anything else is done.
- **What that changes.** Because the system will sit on MAIIC's own network, the automatic read happens entirely inside MAIIC: E-Banker data never leaves MAIIC's network, and no outside party connects to the database. AnyDesk is only for Dupleix's remote help.
- **What comes next.** The work in this guide: the read-only login, tested first on E-Banker's test copy, then on the live system.

### 2.2 How each change reaches MAIIC's server

The copy of the system on MAIIC's server is a copy of the code, so **nothing Dupleix builds reaches it until MAIIC ICT fetches it** (a "pull"). Every piece of new work follows the same five steps before it is tested at MAIIC:

| Step | Who | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Build and prove | Dupleix | The new piece is built and checked, and the bootstrap passes all nine key figures on Dupleix's copy |
| 2. Publish | Dupleix | The new piece is published to the shared code with a note of what it does; MAIIC ICT is told it is ready |
| 3. Fetch onto MAIIC's server | MAIIC ICT, Dupleix watching over AnyDesk | MAIIC ICT fetches the new code onto its server and lets it add any new database tables it needs |
| 4. Re-check on MAIIC's server | MAIIC ICT, with Dupleix | The bootstrap is run on MAIIC's server; all nine key figures must agree there before any testing |
| 5. Test | MAIIC ICT and Dupleix | The tests for that step (section 9) |

If step 4 fails, nothing is tested; Dupleix fixes the problem and the steps start again. The live system is only updated the same way, after the tests pass, and never by copying files onto the server by hand. The history of the shared code shows exactly what was running on MAIIC's server on any date.

## 3. The five ways data can reach the system

There are five ways the data can travel from E-Banker to the IFRS 9 system. They differ only in **who** fetches the data and **how** it travels. Whatever the way, it ends up in the same place and is checked in the same way, and the hand method always stays available as a backup.

| Way | In everyday terms | Where it stands |
|---|---|---|
| **1. By hand, supervised** | MAIIC ICT runs the queries on its own computer while Dupleix watches over AnyDesk, and shares the files | What happens today |
| **2. Scheduled program** | A small program on a MAIIC computer fetches the data at a set time each month and drops the files in a shared folder | Ready on our side; needs the login and the folder |
| **3. Sent to the system's "letterbox"** | The same program posts the files straight to a secure address on the IFRS 9 system, with a secret code, instead of using a folder | Ready on our side; needs the secret code |
| **4. The system reads it directly** (what we are asking for) | The IFRS 9 system, on MAIIC's own server, connects to E-Banker and fetches the data itself | About a week to build once the login exists |
| **5. Through the vendor** | Virtual Galaxy provides a ready-made window onto the data, and the system reads that | Only if the vendor will not allow way 4; likely a paid job |

Ways 2 and 4 use the **same login**, so we would start with way 2 (no new software anywhere) while waiting for the vendor's agreement to way 4.

![Figure 1. Five ways in, one checkpoint. Whatever way the data travels, it passes the same checks before the system uses it.](Feed routes and landing zone - diagram.png)

### 3.1 Way 3 explained: the "letterbox"

The IFRS 9 system has a secure address that accepts deliveries of data, rather like a locked letterbox; in technical terms an **endpoint**. Under way 3, MAIIC's program fetches the data, packs it into one compressed file and posts it to this letterbox over an encrypted connection, with a long secret code (the **token**) that proves it comes from MAIIC.

The letterbox checks four things the moment a delivery arrives: that the secret code is right, that the file is a proper compressed file, that nothing inside it tries to write where it should not, and that it carries its list of contents. If any check fails, the delivery is refused on the spot and nothing is kept. If all pass, it replies "received" at once (technically "202 Accepted") and puts the delivery in a holding tray. Early the next morning the system takes it through the same checkpoint as every other delivery (section 4). Every delivery, accepted or refused, is recorded with the address of the computer that sent it.

![Figure 3. Way 3 step by step: the MAIIC program reads E-Banker, posts the packed file to the system's letterbox, the letterbox checks it and replies at once, and the checkpoint takes it in the next morning.](Route 3 - push by API endpoint - sequence diagram.png)

Before way 3 is used for real, four safeguards would be added, about a day's work: accept deliveries only from MAIIC's own computer; allow the secret code to be changed without a gap; take deliveries through the checkpoint as soon as they arrive rather than the next morning; and refuse oversized deliveries clearly.

**Who opens the connection, and who holds the password.** With the system on MAIIC's server, every way keeps the connection inside MAIIC's network. The difference is who holds the E-Banker password:

| Way | Who starts it | Who holds the E-Banker password | What the IFRS 9 system holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. By hand | A person at MAIIC | MAIIC ICT | Nothing |
| 2. Scheduled program | MAIIC's scheduled task | A locked store on MAIIC's computer | Permission to read the shared folder |
| 3. Letterbox | MAIIC's scheduled task | A locked store on MAIIC's computer | Only the secret code for its letterbox |
| 4. Direct read | The IFRS 9 system's timetable | The IFRS 9 system's settings, on MAIIC's server | The read-only password |
| 5. Through the vendor | The IFRS 9 system's timetable | The IFRS 9 system's settings | The vendor's access details |

Way 4 is the simplest to run, with no program to look after at MAIIC. Ways 2 and 3 suit a policy that the reporting system itself should not hold a database password.

## 4. The "landing zone": a checkpoint at the door

All data from E-Banker passes through one checkpoint inside the system before anything is calculated from it: the **landing zone**. Think of a receiving bay in a warehouse: every delivery is counted and inspected before it goes onto the shelves, and a delivery that fails is set aside, not used.

**Why it is built this way.** One set of checks applies to every way the data arrives. Nothing is ever overwritten, so any month reported in the past can be reproduced exactly. Bad data stops at the door and can never reach the figures. Every figure can be traced back to the delivery, the file and the record it came from. And changing the way data arrives changes nothing in how the figures are calculated.

**What happens to each delivery, step by step.**

1. The delivery arrives with its list of contents: what each file is, how many records it holds and its fingerprint.
2. The system checks whether it has seen this exact delivery before; if so, it is not loaded twice.
3. Each file is checked (complete, unaltered, dates and amounts readable, the question it answers is a known one) and then the files are checked against each other (every payment belongs to a known loan, balances agree with the ledger, every loan has its month-end record, fees agree with the trial balance).
4. If a serious check fails, the whole delivery is **set aside** with the problem named; it is kept so it can be examined, but no figure uses it.
5. If all pass, each record is stored exactly as E-Banker sent it, and a corrected record is added as a new version beside the old one, never over it.
6. The system notes how far it has got for each question (the **watermark**), so the next delivery fetches only what is new.
7. Only then are the monthly loan book and every calculation built from the stored records.

### 4.1 Inside the checkpoint: four record books

The checkpoint keeps four record books in the system's own database:

- **The register**: the list of questions the system is allowed to ask E-Banker, 114 of them after the tenth batch. A question not in the register is not accepted.
- **The deliveries book**: one line for every delivery: when it came, which way, whether it was accepted, the result of every check, and how far it got.
- **The files book**: one line for every file in a delivery: how many records it promised, how many were stored, and how many were new, changed or already held.
- **The records book**: the records themselves, each kept exactly as E-Banker sent it, with every later correction added as a new version beside the old one.

Figure 4 follows one real payment through the four books: MUSECO's K200,000,000 repayment of 24 July 2025. In E-Banker it is ledger record 194427; it arrived in delivery 1 in a file that promised 3,640 records and delivered 3,640; it sits in the records book as version 1, with all 83 of E-Banker's columns as they were. If E-Banker later corrected it to K195,000,000, the original would be kept and marked as replaced, and the corrected one added as version 2: October's figures would still reproduce exactly, and November's would use the correction.

![Figure 4. One payment followed through the four record books of the checkpoint, and what happens if E-Banker later corrects it.](Landing zone - the four tables, one payment followed through - diagram.png)

**Questions MAIIC can answer from the four books**, without asking Dupleix:

| Question | Where the answer is |
|---|---|
| Did this month's delivery arrive, and was it accepted? | The deliveries book |
| Was any file short or altered? | The files book: records promised against records stored, and the fingerprint |
| Which E-Banker record is behind a figure in a report? | The records book: the E-Banker record number, its delivery, its version |
| Has E-Banker changed a record already received? | The records book: any record with a second version, and when the first was replaced |
| What exactly did we ask E-Banker for? | The register: each question, its version and its fingerprint |

The four books already exist in the system's test copies, holding the data received so far (the test copy holds 88,977 records from 23 deliveries), and they are created empty when the system is set up for real on MAIIC's server.

## 5. What the login will and will not do

| It will | It will not |
|---|---|
| Ask only the 114 registered questions, all kept in MAIIC's copy of the code | Change, add or delete anything |
| Run once a month on the first working day after month-end, early in the morning; the overdue table optionally daily | Run any of E-Banker's own programs or change its settings |
| Read a few megabytes a month: MAIIC's own loan schemes and the Mega Farm programme, their payments, balances, repayment schedules, arrears and the trial balance | Read any other customer's accounts, or any table not on the agreed list |
| Connect from one named computer on MAIIC's network, with the password held by MAIIC ICT and changed every 90 days | Connect from anywhere else, or be used by a person |

MAIIC ICT can see everything the login does and can switch it off at any moment. The hand method keeps working regardless.

## 6. Setting up the login: the steps for MAIIC ICT

MAIIC ICT does the same steps twice: first on E-Banker's **test copy**, and later on the **live system** (or its reporting copy), only after the tests on the test copy have passed. The technical document gives the exact commands for each step; here is what each one achieves.

1. **Agree the names.** The login, a "role" that holds its permissions, and a profile that limits it. The computer it connects from is the MAIIC server the system is installed on.
2. **Create the limits.** A profile that allows at most two connections at a time, locks the login after five wrong passwords and forces a new password every 90 days.
3. **Create the login.** It can sign in and own nothing; it has no space of its own, so it cannot create anything.
4. **Give it read permission, table by table.** One line per table on the agreed list (51 tables, set out in the annex), all held in one role so the whole access can be removed with one command. If a table is not where expected, MAIIC ICT tells us and we correct the list.
5. **Switch on monitoring.** E-Banker's database records every sign-in and every question the login asks, so MAIIC can see everything it does.
6. **Open the network path.** One firewall rule: the system's server may reach the database, and nothing else changes.
7. **Test the connection.** From the computer that will use the login: is the database reachable on the network; can the login sign in; and a short test question that answers "who am I, which database am I in, which computer am I calling from, and what time is it". The database name is the most important answer: it must say **test** at the test stage and **live** at the live stage, never the other way round. A first real question then counts MAIIC's loan accounts.
8. **Prove it is read-only.** The login lists its own permissions (only "sign in"); it can see only the agreed tables; a harmless attempt to delete must be refused; an attempt to create a table must be refused; and the two checks from the tenth batch (which tables it can read, and that every one of the 35 tables answers) must pass. The results are saved as evidence.
9. **Hand over safely.** The database address may be emailed; the password never is. It is typed into the system's settings by MAIIC ICT, or kept in a locked store on MAIIC's computer under ways 2 and 3.
10. **For way 2 or 3 only.** A small Oracle tool and a scheduled task on a MAIIC computer (way 2), or permission for that computer to post to the system's letterbox and a secret code kept in Windows' locked store (way 3), tested once with a wrong code to prove it is refused.
11. **Look after it.** A new password every 90 days; the login can be paused at once and resumed, or removed entirely; any new table needs a one-line permission that MAIIC approves.
12. **Repeat on the live system** once the tests pass, with a new password, and run the connection test and read-only proof again.

## 7. What we need from the vendor

The login is within MAIIC's own control, but we ask Virtual Galaxy to confirm in writing that a read-only login used this way does not affect their support agreement; whether they prefer us to read a copy of the database rather than the live one; whether they need any extra monitoring; and whether there is any cost. If they will not allow it, we ask them to quote for way 5. Two questions go to them in any case: their report of restructured loans (the restructure table in E-Banker is empty, although the migration records show eight), and where write-offs are recorded (the write-off table is empty, although the ledger shows write-off postings).

## 8. The bootstrap: our test copy and safety check

The **bootstrap** is a single command that builds a complete copy of the IFRS 9 system from scratch on a separate test database, in about two minutes. It never touches the live system, and nothing approved inside it counts as a MAIIC approval. In order, it:

1. **Wipes** the test database and creates it afresh.
2. **Loads** every batch MAIIC has sent, and Finance's fee template, take-on workbook and trial balances, through the same checkpoint as the live system.
3. **Builds** the monthly loan books, contract details, fees and interest schedules.
4. **Runs every calculation**: staging, probability of default, loss given default, expected credit loss, interest revenue, forward-looking adjustments, stress tests, reports and the general ledger reconciliation.
5. **Checks nine key figures** that must agree exactly with an independent source: the interest posted in the ledger; the loan balances against E-Banker's own loan book report, for every account and month; the year-end interest entries on two income accounts; and the loan balances against the trial balance on each of the five loan accounts in the general ledger. Today all nine agree.

![Figure 2. The bootstrap builds the system on a test copy and checks nine key figures; only when they agree does a change reach the live system.](Bootstrap - test harness and reference copy - diagram.png)

It plays five parts in this work:

| Part | What it means |
|---|---|
| **The history** | The batches copied by hand since 7 October are the history up to the switch; the bootstrap builds it, the same way every time, and the automatic read continues from where it ends |
| **The test copy** | The automatic read is first connected to the bootstrap's database, never to the live one |
| **The yardstick** | The bootstrap already holds each month as it arrived by hand; the automatic read must reproduce it exactly, record for record |
| **The safety check** | Before any change reaches the live system, including each pull onto MAIIC's server (section 2.2), the bootstrap is run and all nine key figures must still agree |
| **The fire drill** | Each quarter, a backup is restored and checked the same way |

## 9. Test first, then go live

Nothing touches real E-Banker data until the whole arrangement has worked on a copy.

1. **Install (stage 0).** The system is set up on MAIIC's server and the bootstrap is run there: all nine key figures must agree.
2. **Approve (stage A).** Dr Thom approves; MAIIC writes to the vendor.
3. **Test on a copy (stage B).** MAIIC ICT creates the login on E-Banker's test copy. Each piece of new work is fetched onto MAIIC's server and re-checked (section 2.2). Way 2 runs first, then way 4. Seven tests are signed off by MAIIC ICT and Dupleix: (1) the connection test passes and nothing outside the agreed list can be read; (2) the automatic read gives exactly the same records as the hand method for the same month; (3) reading the same month again adds nothing; (4) a deliberately broken file is caught and nothing downstream moves; (5) a monthly read takes under 15 minutes with no noticeable load on E-Banker; (6) a backup can be restored and carried on from; (7) the bootstrap, re-run with the automatically read data, still agrees on all nine key figures.
4. **Go live (stage C).** The login is created on the live system and the setting is switched to way 4, which needs two people to approve.
5. **Run side by side.** For two month-ends both methods are used and must agree exactly before the hand method is retired; it remains available as a backup.

If the vendor declines way 4, the same steps run on way 2, which needs nothing from the vendor.

### 9.1 Why this must be planned now

The building takes about a week; the time is taken by things outside it, in a fixed order:

- **Approvals and the vendor take weeks.** Dr Thom's approval, the vendor's written confirmation and MAIIC's own change control for a new login and a firewall rule all come first.
- **A test copy of E-Banker has to exist.** If there is none, one must be made from a backup, which needs ICT and vendor time.
- **Proof needs real month-ends, and there is only one a month.** Missing November moves the switch from January to February; every missed month-end moves it by a month.
- **Year-end matters most.** The December 2026 year-end feeds the annual accounts and Deloitte's audit; running both methods side by side on it gives the auditors the strongest evidence.
- **Year-end change freezes.** Many ICT teams freeze changes over December, so everything that changes MAIIC's systems is planned to finish by 27 November.
- **The hand method is a risk every month it remains the only one.** Every batch so far has needed a re-run, and the overdue table cannot be copied by hand at all.

Assuming approval by **Friday 23 October 2026**. Each week of delay moves every later date; missing a month-end moves the switch by a whole month.

| When | What |

| 15 to 23 October | The system is set up on MAIIC's server and the bootstrap run there; Dr Thom approves; MAIIC writes to the vendor |
| 26 October to 6 November | MAIIC ICT sets up the test login and the connection test; the scheduled program is fetched onto MAIIC's server and installed on the test copy; vendor reply expected by 6 November |
| 2 November | October month-end copied by hand, as now |
| 2 to 13 November | Dupleix builds the direct read (way 4) |
| 13 November | The new work is fetched onto MAIIC's server and the bootstrap re-run there |

| 23 to 27 November | The login is created on the live system, before any year-end change freeze |

![Figure 5. The proposed timetable, from setting the system up on MAIIC's server in October 2026 to the first month-end read automatically in February 2027.](Route 4 - proposed build and test timetable - gantt.png)

## 10. How the data is kept up to date

Every question the system asks E-Banker is written down in the register, with a version number and a fingerprint, and the register is kept in the system's code; a question is changed by changing the code, not by editing a worksheet. There are two kinds of table:

- **Reference tables are read in full each time** (the list of accounts, the loan terms, the repayment schedules in force, security, rates). They are small, and only records that are new or changed are stored.
- **History tables are read from where the last delivery stopped** (payments, balances, the monthly loan book report, the overdue calculation, interest). The watermark records the last record received, so the next read fetches only what is new. Under the hand method the watermark is printed on the batch sheet; under the automatic read the system applies it itself.

A month can be read again at any time (a correction, a late posting) and the same rules apply. If a question is changed, it gets a new version number; a file produced by an old version is refused, so an outdated query cannot feed the system unnoticed.

## 11. How duplicates are handled

Duplicates are caught at three levels, automatically, and nothing is ever overwritten:

| Level | How it is recognised | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **The whole delivery** | Its fingerprint | A delivery already loaded is recognised and not loaded again |
| **Each file** | Its fingerprint, its record count, and no record number repeated inside it | A short, altered or doubled file is refused, with the problem named |
| **Each record** | E-Banker's own record number and a fingerprint of its contents | Same number and same contents: skipped. Same number, new contents: stored as a new version, the old one kept. New number: stored |

So when two questions overlap (for example the month-end and the daily overdue records), each record is stored once. Every delivery shows how many records were new, changed or already held, so a fully duplicated delivery shows "nothing new" rather than counting twice.

## 12. The controls around the data

- **Checks before anything moves.** A delivery that fails a serious check is set aside whole; nothing downstream moves.
- **Only accepted deliveries are used**, and every calculation records which deliveries it used, so a figure can be traced to its source.
- **A full record.** Every delivery, accepted or set aside, is recorded with who or what delivered it, and the fingerprints let an auditor confirm a file is the one E-Banker produced.
- **Closed months stay closed.** Once a month is locked, a late delivery still lands but its effect is taken in the open month, with the difference shown.
- **Two people to change the way data arrives**, with an effective date; the hand method always stays available.
- **Changes to the questions** only through the controlled code, checked on arrival.
- **Changes to the system** only by the release steps of section 2.2.
- **The login is MAIIC's**: created, held, changed and revocable by MAIIC ICT, and visible in E-Banker's own records.

## 13. Keeping the data safe: storage and backup

**Where it is kept.** Nothing is stored in E-Banker; the login only reads. The data is kept in the IFRS 9 system's own database on MAIIC's server: the checkpoint's records (85 MB for about two years of MAIIC's loans today), the calculated tables (24 MB, which can be rebuilt from the records), and the delivered files themselves (87 MB so far), about 110 MB in all.

**Growth.** A month adds 3 to 5 MB. The full Mega Farm ledger will add 300 to 400 MB once. The daily overdue record adds 120 to 150 MB a year for MAIIC's own loans; for the Mega Farm programme (3,675 accounts) only the month-end records are read, because the daily ones would be 1.3 million a year. The database should stay under 2 GB for five years; the server needs at least 20 GB free, with an alert when it is 80 percent full.

**How long it is kept.** For the life of the system, never deleted, because past figures must be reproducible. That is longer than the seven years required for accounting records.

| Backup | How often | How many kept | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| A full copy of the database | Every night, after the morning delivery | 30 daily, 12 month-end and 7 year-end copies | On the server and off it, in MAIIC's backup store |
| A copy taken when each month is closed | Monthly | All, permanently | Off the server, with the month's delivered files |
| The delivered files | As each arrives | All, permanently | MAIIC's document store |
| The questions and the system's code | Every change | The full history | The shared code, which MAIIC holds a copy of |

Every backup is **encrypted**, because it holds customer loan data, and a **test restore** is done every quarter. The passwords and the backup key are held by MAIIC ICT, not by Dupleix. If the database were lost, it would be restored from the last night's copy and anything since read again from E-Banker; the watermarks say where to start and the duplicate rules make the re-read safe.

## Annex: what the login reads, and why

The full list of 51 tables, with the questions that use each one, is in the annex of the technical document. Grouped by what they hold:

| Group | E-Banker tables | Why the system needs them |
|---|---|---|
| **Customers, accounts and loan terms** | Account master, loan master, customer master, scheme master | Which loans are MAIIC's and the Mega Farm programme's; their amounts, rates, terms and repayment holidays |
| **Money movements** | The ledger (every posting) | Disbursements, interest, repayments, write-offs and fees: the actual cash flows behind every figure, including loans paid off from new loans |
| **Balances and the monthly loan book** | Balance history, E-Banker's stored loan book report | Each loan's balance and arrears at every month-end, checked against the ledger |
| **Repayment schedules** | Instalment chart, instalment plans, disbursement schedules | What each borrower should pay and when; when undrawn amounts become exposure |
| **Arrears** | E-Banker's daily overdue calculation | How many days each loan is overdue, checked independently of the loan book report |
| **Status and closures** | Status history, closures, change log | Whether a loan is active, closed or written off, and when terms changed |
| **Rates and interest** | Rate set-up, interest products, prime rate history, interest calculated, accrued and waived | The contractual rate and its changes; E-Banker's own interest against the system's |
| **Fees** | Disbursement charges, charge postings, loan application records | Fees charged at the start of a loan, which change the effective interest rate |
| **Security** | Security details, guarantors | Collateral, which reduces the expected loss |
| **Restructures and write-offs** | Reschedule details, write-off records | Loans whose terms were changed, and loans written off |
| **The general ledger** | GL chart, GL opening balances, trial balance history | Tying the loan book to MAIIC's accounts each month |
| **History, read once** | Older ledger copies, earlier repayment schedules, the July 2024 migration tables, the account list of 5 August 2024 | The history before E-Banker's July 2024 migration, and how old account numbers map to new ones |

Every question is limited to MAIIC's own loan schemes and the Mega Farm programme, so no other customer's data is read.

## Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **E-Banker** | MAIIC's core banking system, where loans, payments and the general ledger are recorded. Supplied and supported by Virtual Galaxy. |
| **IFRS 9 system** | The system Dupleix is building for MAIIC to calculate expected credit losses, interest revenue and the regulatory figures from E-Banker's data. |
| **Oracle** | The database software E-Banker stores its data in. |
| **Database** | The organised store of records behind a system. E-Banker has one; the IFRS 9 system has its own. |
| **Server** | A computer that runs a system for others to use. The IFRS 9 system is being set up on a MAIIC server. |
| **Production (live)** | The real system and data used for MAIIC's reporting. |
| **Test copy (test environment, UAT)** | A separate copy of a system used for trying things out, so mistakes cannot affect the real data. |
| **Replica (reporting copy)** | A continuously updated copy of the live database, used for reporting so the live system is not disturbed. |
| **Code repository** | The shared, controlled store of the system's code. MAIIC ICT has access and has copied it onto MAIIC's server. |
| **Pull (fetch)** | Copying the latest published changes from the code repository onto MAIIC's server. Nothing new reaches MAIIC's server until it is pulled. |
| **AnyDesk** | Remote-desktop software that lets Dupleix watch, and help with, work on a MAIIC computer. |
| **Query (question)** | A precise request for data from a database, such as "all payments on MAIIC's loans since 1 September". |
| **Register** | The controlled list of every question the system may ask E-Banker, 114 after the tenth batch. |
| **Read-only login** | A username and password that can look at data but cannot change it. |
| **Role** | A named set of permissions given to a login, so all of them can be granted or removed at once. |
| **Grant** | Permission given to a login to read a particular table. |
| **Table** | One set of records in a database, such as the list of loan accounts or the list of payments. |
| **Firewall** | The network gatekeeper that decides which computers may connect to which. |
| **VPN** | A secure, encrypted connection between two organisations' networks, used for Dupleix's remote support. |
| **Feed route (way)** | The way data travels from E-Banker to the IFRS 9 system; one of the five in section 3. |
| **Batch (pack)** | One delivery of data: one file per question, plus a list of what the files should contain. |
| **Manifest** | The list that comes with each batch, stating how many records each file holds and its fingerprint. |
| **Fingerprint (hash)** | A short code calculated from a file's exact contents; if even one character changes, the code changes, so it proves a file is complete and unaltered. |
| **API** | A way for one computer system to send requests or data to another automatically. |
| **Endpoint ("letterbox")** | A specific secure address on a system that accepts deliveries from another computer. |
| **Token (secret code)** | A long secret code sent with each delivery to prove who it comes from; a password for a computer rather than a person. |
| **HTTPS** | The encrypted form of web traffic, so data cannot be read on the way. |
| **Push and pull** | Push: the sender delivers the data (ways 2 and 3). Pull: the receiver fetches it (ways 4 and 5). |
| **202 Accepted** | The letterbox's reply when a delivery is received and waiting to be checked; not yet a confirmation that it passed. |
| **Landing zone (checkpoint)** | The place inside the IFRS 9 system where every delivery is checked and stored before any calculation uses it. |
| **Gates (checks)** | The tests every delivery must pass at the checkpoint. |
| **Quarantine (set aside)** | Keeping a delivery that failed a check for inspection, without ever using it. |
| **Version** | A record as it stood at a point in time. When E-Banker changes a record, the old version is kept and the new one added. |
| **Watermark** | A marker of the last record already received, so the next delivery fetches only what is new. |
| **Bootstrap** | The command that rebuilds the whole IFRS 9 system from scratch on a test database and checks the key figures. |
| **Golden ties (key figures)** | The nine figures the bootstrap checks against an independent source; all must agree exactly. |
| **Maker-checker** | A control where one person proposes a change and a second person must approve it. |
| **Period lock** | Closing a reporting month so its figures cannot change afterwards. |
| **Change freeze** | A period, often over year-end, when ICT makes no changes to live systems. |
| **Audit trail** | The record of who or what did what, and when, kept for the auditors. |
| **Trial balance** | The list of every general ledger account's balance at a date. |
| **Mega Farm** | The farming programme whose loans MAIIC administers alongside its own loan book. |
| **Virtual Galaxy** | The company that supplies and supports E-Banker. |
| **Dupleix** | Dupleix Institute, the firm building the IFRS 9 system for MAIIC. |
